levels.headline: FTSE 100 edges up on Friday but ends a week of gilt turmoil down 2.18%
levels.body:
The FTSE 100 closed on Friday 2 October at 10,461.95, up 33.68 points, or 0.32%, from Thursday's close of 10,428.27. Even so, the index of the UK's largest listed companies fell 2.18% over the week.
Thursday was the weak spot. The FTSE 100 fell about 1.7%, its worst day since May, as the UK government bond market sold off. The yield (interest rate) on 30-year gilts touched 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing to about 5.9% by the close.
On Friday the 10-year gilt yield fell about nine basis points (0.09 percentage points) after a weak US jobs report, and the pound rose 0.2% to about $1.3226.
The gilt sell-off has been driven by inflation worries linked to the Iran war and rising expectations of interest rate rises. When yields rise, it costs the government more to borrow.
levels.why: Rising gilt yields make government borrowing more expensive, which can affect taxes, spending and the wider economy.

headline: Five arrested near RAF Fairford as Burnham points to Iranian involvement

levels.headline: Five arrested near RAF Fairford as Burnham points to Iranian involvement
levels.body:
Five British men in their 20s, all from London, were arrested early on Sunday 27 September in Whelford, Gloucestershire, after a call about three suspicious vehicles heading towards RAF Fairford, a US-operated air base. They were held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act and of offences under the Explosives Act, and were released on bail on Monday.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there are "strong indications" that Iran played a part. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor". Iran denies any involvement, and its embassy in Britain called the claims unfounded.
Later reports say a 27-year-old man with UK and Iranian nationality was arrested in Westminster on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, and a 26-year-old UK national was questioned. Two London properties were searched.
The US has used RAF Fairford for B-52 and B-1 bombers during the war with Iran. The investigation continues and no one has been convicted.
levels.why: It links a security incident on British soil to the wider war with Iran and to relations between London and Washington.

headline: Bond market sell-off has roughly halved Healey's room for manoeuvre ahead of Budget

terms.meaning: The gap between the government's planned spending and the limits the Chancellor has set himself. It is his room for manoeuvre.
When tax thresholds are frozen, so more people pay more tax as their wages rise.
The interest rate the government pays to borrow by selling bonds called gilts.

levels.headline: Bond market sell-off has roughly halved Healey's room for manoeuvre ahead of Budget
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first Budget on 28 October. He has said he will not reveal his plans before then.
Analysts at Pantheon Macroeconomics calculated that the global bond market sell-off has cut his fiscal headroom (the gap between planned spending and the limits he set himself) from £23.6bn at the Spring Statement to roughly £13bn. Economists estimate he needs to find about £10bn through tax rises or spending cuts.
Manifesto promises protect the main tax rates, but not capital gains, inheritance tax, property, fuel duty or fiscal drag (freezing tax thresholds), so analysts see these as open to change. Speculation has grown about a mansion tax and changes to capital gains.
As of the September reporting, 10-year gilt yields had reached around 5.2%, the highest in 18 years, and 30-year yields were around 5.9%.
levels.why: The Budget will decide which taxes and spending change, and higher borrowing costs have made that choice harder.

headline: Markets see 87% chance of Bank of England rate rise on 5 November

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate. It influences the rates on mortgages, loans and savings.

The gap between two percentages, so a rise from 3.75% to 4.00% is 0.25 percentage points.

levels.headline: Markets see 87% chance of Bank of England rate rise on 5 November
levels.body:
The Bank of England held Bank Rate at 3.75% at its 17 September meeting. Its next decision is on 5 November, and markets put the chance of a 0.25 percentage point rise to 4.00% at around 87%.
On 25 September Governor Andrew Bailey said the Bank "hasn't increased bank rates" but that it is "going to get harder to maintain that stance as energy prices remain higher". Energy prices are high because of the Iran war.
Andrew Goodwin, chief economist at Oxford Economics, expects rises of 0.25 points in November and February, which would take Bank Rate to 4.25%.
A higher Bank Rate makes mortgages and loans cost more and makes savings pay more. The Bank uses it to bring inflation down.
levels.why: Changes to Bank Rate affect what people pay on mortgages and loans and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Markets price in a likely Bank of England rate rise in November
levels.body:
The Bank of England kept Bank Rate at 3.75% at its meeting on 17 September. The next decision comes on 5 November. Markets put the chance of a 0.25 percentage point rise to 4.00% at around 87%.
Governor Andrew Bailey said on 25 September that the Bank "hasn't increased bank rates", but that it is "going to get harder to maintain that stance as energy prices remain higher". Energy prices are high because of the Iran war.
Oxford Economics chief economist Andrew Goodwin expects rises of 0.25 points in both November and February, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%.
A higher Bank Rate makes mortgages and loans cost more, and savings pay more. The Bank uses it to bring inflation down.
levels.why: A rise would raise mortgage and loan costs for many households while improving returns for savers.

levels.headline: The Bank might make borrowing cost a bit more
levels.body:

headline: Burnham cuts VAT on household electricity to zero from 1 October

terms.meaning: Value Added Tax, a tax added to the price of most goods and services, charged here on household electricity at 5%.

levels.headline: Burnham cuts VAT on household electricity to zero from 1 October
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cut VAT on household electricity from 5% to 0% from 1 October 2026, in England, Scotland and Wales. It saves the average household about £45 a year and is due to last until the end of the financial year in March 2027.
The government says the cut is paid for by cancelling the previous government's digital ID scheme, which it puts at about £1.8bn. Critics say that scheme never had money set aside in the Treasury's books, so they question whether the saving is real.
At Labour's conference in Liverpool, Burnham also announced a publicly owned "Great British Grid" to challenge private energy network operators.
Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July 2026, after Keir Starmer announced his resignation on 22 June.
levels.why: It lowers energy bills for millions of homes and shows how the new government plans to pay for its policies.

He said Iran had been "decimated" and faced "the easy way or the hard way". Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said Trump keeps "all the options he needs on the table" and that "Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon".

headline: G7 to release up to 100 million barrels of oil reserves as diesel stocks are tapped

terms.meaning: Emergency stocks of fuel that governments hold for times when supplies are short.
A widely used benchmark price for oil, quoted in dollars a barrel.
An international body that helps its member countries coordinate on energy supplies.

levels.headline: G7 to release up to 100 million barrels of oil reserves as diesel stocks are tapped
levels.body:
The G7 group of rich countries said on Friday 2 October that it will release up to 100 million barrels of strategic oil reserves over the next four months. The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency (IEA) and includes a "frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days".
European governments agreed to release diesel from emergency stocks after US President Donald Trump pressed them to do so, reportedly threatening a fuel export ban. Strategic reserves are emergency fuel stocks that governments hold for times of supply trouble.
Oil prices fell about $2 on the news, and Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped to around $99 a barrel. Diesel prices have risen because of the Iran war and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route for oil.
Analysts quoted say a large diesel release could cut wholesale prices by $20 to $30 a barrel, which they put at roughly 10 to 15 euro cents per litre at the pump.
levels.why: Diesel moves freight and farming costs, so cheaper supplies could ease pressure on prices well beyond the petrol station.

levels.headline: Weak US jobs figures lift Wall Street as investors expect no Fed rate rise

headline: High energy prices push up UK household costs as Bank of England weighs a rate rise

levels.headline: High energy prices push up UK household costs as Bank of England weighs a rate rise
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.1% in August, a five-month high, driven by fuel prices, according to the Office for National Statistics. Inflation measures how fast prices are rising.
Bank Rate, the Bank of England's main interest rate, stands at 3.75%. Governor Andrew Bailey said on 25 September that keeping rates unchanged would get "harder to maintain" if energy prices stay high. ING says the Bank has floated a November rise if energy prices do not come down.
Brent crude is near $100 a barrel, or about $99 after Friday's G7 reserve release news. Higher fuel and energy costs push up prices in shops and for businesses.
Households have some relief. From 1 October, VAT on household electricity fell from 5% to 0%, saving the average household about £45 a year until March 2027. A rate rise would be a further squeeze for anyone with a variable-rate mortgage or loan, though the Bank has not made that decision.
levels.why: Energy prices shape both the cost of living and the cost of borrowing for UK households.

headline: UK services growth slows to 51.7 in September, but manufacturing picks up

terms.meaning: Purchasing Managers' Index, a survey of firms. A score above 50 means activity is growing.
An early reading published before the final figures, based on most of the survey replies.
Businesses that sell services rather than goods, such as shops, restaurants, banks and travel firms.

levels.headline: UK services growth slows to 51.7 in September, but manufacturing picks up
levels.body:
S&P Global's flash UK PMI (Purchasing Managers' Index, a survey of firms where a reading above 50 means growth) showed services sector activity slowing to 51.7 in September from 52.5 in August. That was below the 52.0 that had been expected.
Manufacturing moved the other way. Its PMI rose to 52.0 from 51.7, above the 51.4 expected.
Reports on the survey, which also covers the wider mood among firms, describe sluggish growth, rising inflation pressure, subdued business confidence and high costs discouraging hiring.
These are the flash estimates, which were published on 23 September. They are an early reading, and both sectors remain above the 50 line that separates growth from contraction.
levels.why: The surveys give an early sign of how firms are coping, including whether they are likely to hire.

levels.headline: UK flash PMI shows services slowing, manufacturing improving
levels.body:
The flash UK PMI from S&P Global, a survey of firms in which a score above 50 signals growth, showed services sector activity easing to 51.7 in September from 52.5 in August. Economists had expected 52.0.
Manufacturing, the sector that makes goods, improved. Its PMI rose to 52.0 from 51.7 and beat the 51.4 forecast.
Reports on the survey describe sluggish growth, rising inflation pressure, subdued business confidence and high costs that discourage hiring.
The figures are flash estimates, meaning an early reading based on most of the replies, published on 23 September. They come early in the reporting cycle, and both sectors remain above 50, which marks the line between growth and contraction.
levels.why: Hiring and price pressures in these surveys feed into jobs, wages and inflation.

levels.headline: UK services growth slows in September while factories pick up
levels.body:
Activity in the UK services sector grew more slowly in September, according to the flash PMI from S&P Global. The PMI is a survey of firms, and a reading above 50 means growth. Services slipped to 51.7 from 52.5 in August, below the 52.0 that was expected.
Manufacturing did better. Its PMI rose to 52.0 from 51.7 and came in above the forecast of 51.4.
Reports on the survey describe sluggish growth, rising pressure on prices, low business confidence and high costs that put firms off hiring.
These are flash estimates, published on 23 September. Both readings stay above 50, so both sectors are still growing, though not by much.
levels.why: They show whether businesses feel confident enough to hire and invest.

levels.headline: UK service firms grew more slowly in September
levels.body:
A monthly survey of businesses, called the PMI, shows how the UK economy is doing. A score above 50 means growth. In September the score for services firms fell to 51.7 from 52.5 in August. Experts had expected 52.0.
Factories did better. Their score rose to 52.0 from 51.7, above the 51.4 that was expected.
Reports on the survey say growth is sluggish. Prices are putting more pressure on firms, business confidence is low, and high costs are making firms less likely to hire.
These figures are an early estimate, known as a flash estimate, published on 23 September. Both scores are above 50, so both areas are still growing, but only slowly.
levels.why: The results hint at whether jobs and prices will be under pressure in coming months.

levels.headline: UK businesses report slower growth in September
levels.body:
Each month a survey asks UK firms how busy they are. The result is called the PMI. A score over 50 means firms are growing. A score under 50 means they are shrinking.
In September the score for service firms, such as shops, banks and restaurants, fell to 51.7. In August it was 52.5. Experts had thought it would be 52.0.
The score for factories went up to 52.0 from 51.7. That was better than the 51.4 that experts expected.
The survey says growth is slow. Prices are rising. Firms feel unsure about the future. High costs mean they are less keen to hire new people.
These numbers are early estimates, published on 23 September. Both scores are still over 50.
levels.why: If firms feel unsure and stop hiring, it can be harder for people to find jobs.

These are early numbers, from 23 September. Both scores are still over 50. So businesses are still growing, but slowly.
levels.why: Slower growth and less hiring can affect how easy it is for people to find work.

levels.why: It helps us see if businesses are doing well, and if there will be jobs.

levels.headline: UK businesses are busy, but growing slowly
levels.body:
Every month, people ask UK businesses a question. How busy are you? The answers are turned into a number. If the number is over 50, businesses are busier. If it is under 50, they are less busy.
In September, places like shops, banks and restaurants got 51.7. In August it was 52.5. So they are still getting busier, but more slowly than before. Factories, where things are made, got 52.0. That was a little better than before.
The survey says prices are going up. Businesses feel a bit unsure. Things cost a lot, so they do not want to hire many new workers.
Both numbers are over 50, so businesses are still growing. But they are not growing fast.
levels.why: If businesses hire fewer workers, it can be harder for grown-ups to find a job.

levels.headline: UK businesses are still growing, but slowly
levels.body:
Think of a school running a cake sale each month. Some months it sells lots. Some months it sells fewer. Grown-ups ask businesses the same kind of question each month. They ask how busy they have been.
This time, shops, banks and restaurants said they were still busier. But they were not as busy as the month before. Factories, where things are made, said they were a bit busier than before.
The businesses said that things cost a lot. They also said they were not sure what would happen next. So they did not want to hire many new workers.
The good news is that both groups are still growing. But they are growing slowly, like a plant on a cold day.
levels.why: It shows if businesses are doing well, which helps grown-ups keep their jobs and find new ones.
